title: Bernard Stiegler
keyWorks: Taking Care of Youth and the Generations (2008)
What Makes Life Worth Living: On Pharmacology (2010)
summary: Bernard Stiegler (1952–2020) was a French philosopher of technology and a student of Jacques Derrida. He held that human beings have lived through technics from the very beginning: tools, writing and media are our external memory. In Symbolic Misery and Taking Care of Youth and the Generations he showed how the attention industry and marketing reshape our feelings and desires, and he looked for ways to take back care of them.
onEmotions: Stiegler’s key concept is the pharmakon: a Greek word that means both poison and remedy. Any technology — writing, a smartphone, a news feed, a substance — can both nourish our lives and destroy them; it all depends on how we handle it. Stiegler distinguished “desire,” which is tenderly attached to something singular and knows how to wait, from “drive,” which is short-lived and demands immediate satisfaction. The modern “attention economy” and hyperconsumption, in his view, turn desire into drive and take away our ability to feel and choose for ourselves — this is what he called “the proletarianization of sensibility.” So many painful states are not only a personal problem but also a consequence of our environment; and that means caring for yourself can take the form of learning anew how to live with your pharmaka.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is an understandable response to a world that changes faster than we can get used to it. Stiegler wrote about this in The Age of Disruption. He called our era a time of “disruption”: technologies are updated so rapidly that society, culture and the individual simply can’t develop ways of living with them. He considered this “maladjustment” between technology and life one of the main causes of today’s unease. From this angle, your anxiety isn’t only a personal weakness but also a response to a real break in rhythms. That doesn’t make it lighter, but it can lift some of the guilt: you’re anxious not because something is wrong with you, but because time really has fallen out of step.
anxiety.practice: Write down one thing that’s been changing too fast for you lately, and one thing that has stayed reliably the same.

fear.text: Fear is an ancient protector, and it has a right to exist. Stiegler opened his major work, Technics and Time, with the myth of Prometheus and Epimetheus: when the gods were handing out qualities to the animals — claws, fur, speed — Epimetheus forgot about humans. The human being was born “without qualities,” vulnerable, and so had to rely on fire and crafts — that is, on technics. For Stiegler this original lack isn’t a disgrace but the very essence of being human: we never stand on our own strength alone, but on supports we create and pass on to each other. From this angle, fear reminds you of your vulnerability. But it also points to a way out: not becoming invulnerable, but finding something to lean on — people, knowledge, reliable familiar practices.
fear.practice: Name your fear, then list three supports — people, skills or things — that helped you in a similar situation.

sadness.text: Sadness tells you that something important to you is far away or out of reach right now. Stiegler has a book with a telling title: What Makes Life Worth Living. He believed that life is valuable because of our attachments — to people, activities, places and things we love and care for. Sadness often appears when such attachments weaken or break. From this angle, it isn’t a malfunction but a sign that your capacity to cherish is alive. Stiegler stressed that true desire is always directed at something singular, irreplaceable, and he considered caring for such attachments the main work of life. Sadness shows you where that care is most needed right now.
sadness.practice: Write down what or whom exactly you’re sad about right now. Then ask: how can I take even a little care of this attachment today?

grief.text: Grief is love that has lost its addressee. Stiegler thought a great deal about memory and about how human memory lives not only in our heads. He called everything that holds experience outside us “tertiary retentions”: letters, photographs, voice recordings, objects, habits passed on to others. Thanks to them the past keeps talking to us. From this angle, the person who has died hasn’t vanished without a trace: they remain in the memory inscribed in the world — in words you picked up from them, in things they touched. These traces can hurt, but they are also a way of continuing the bond. Handling them with care doesn’t mean getting stuck in the past; it means caring for what was precious.
grief.practice: Choose one object or recording connected with the person you’ve lost, and spend a few minutes with it. Ask: what of this person do I want to pass on?

loneliness.text: Loneliness is the pain of a broken bond. Drawing on the philosopher Gilbert Simondon, Stiegler held that a person becomes themselves only together with others: “psychic individuation” — the becoming of an “I” — is inseparable from “collective individuation,” the becoming of a “we.” We grow by sharing language, songs, work, common meanings. Stiegler was troubled that today’s media environment replaces this kind of communion with a stream: we see thousands of people but rarely do anything together with them. He called this the loss of the “we.” From this angle, your loneliness isn’t proof that something is wrong with you but part of a large problem of our era. And the way out isn’t in the number of contacts, but in doing something together, however small.
loneliness.practice: Remember one thing you enjoyed doing together with someone — cooking, singing, fixing things. Think about whom you could share it with now.

anger.text: Anger often arises when something precious has been hurt. Stiegler believed that people need love of self in order to live — following psychoanalysis, he called it “primary narcissism” — that is, a basic sense that you matter and that your existence carries weight. When society and media turn people into interchangeable consumers, this foundation wears thin, and rage can build up in its place. This doesn’t justify destructive acts, but it explains where some of today’s anger comes from. From this angle, you can treat your anger with curiosity: might it be telling you that you aren’t being seen or heard? Its energy can be turned toward caring for what truly matters to you.
anger.practice: Finish the sentence: “I’m angry because what matters to me is…”. Read your answer as a pointer to what is worth protecting.

shame.text: Shame makes us hide. Stiegler himself lived through a turn that many would find shameful: as a young man he went to prison for armed robbery and spent five years there. He didn’t hide this part of his life — later he spoke about it openly in his book Acting Out, describing how he began studying philosophy in his cell. For him prison became the place where he learned to read and think anew. From Stiegler’s point of view, a person isn’t a fixed essence but an “individuation,” an ongoing process of becoming. What you’re ashamed of is a moment in that process, not a final definition of you. You can acknowledge shame without making it your prison.
shame.practice: Write down in one sentence what you’re ashamed of. Beneath it write: “And besides that, I am a person who…” — and finish the sentence in three different ways.

guilt.text: Guilt is a sign that you feel responsible. For Stiegler, care is one of the central concepts: we live by caring for one another, for children, for the world, and this care can’t be handed over to a machine. In Taking Care of Youth and the Generations he wrote about the duty of the older toward the younger — to pass on attention, knowledge, the art of living. Guilt is often exactly the painful sense that care somewhere didn’t work out. From this angle, you can take it not as a verdict but as a signpost: here is a place where it matters to you to care better. Stiegler spoke of care as a practice one learns all one’s life, and in any practice mistakes are inevitable. What matters is coming back to it.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: whom or what is my guilt about? Write down one small step of care you could take now.

envy.text: Envy squeezes painfully: it seems others have something without which you are incomplete. Stiegler would draw attention to where much of what we want comes from. He wrote that mass media and advertising “synchronize consciousnesses”: millions of people watch the same thing at the same time and begin to desire the same things. So desire loses its singularity and turns into a race of comparisons. For Stiegler, genuine desire is always directed at something singular, while the industry offers interchangeable goods. From this angle, envy is partly an effect of the environment, not your personal flaw. Beneath it there may be a desire of your own, a real one, worth separating from the imposed one.
envy.practice: Ask yourself: would I want this if no one could ever know about it? Write down what remains after that question.

emptiness.text: Apathy and emptiness are heavy: as if everything has lost its taste. Stiegler described a similar state of a whole society with the words “symbolic misery.” It isn’t a lack of things, but a lack of the chance to take part yourself in making meanings — songs, images, stories, rituals. When we only consume what has been made for us, our sensibility, for Stiegler, is “proletarianized”: just as a worker on an assembly line loses their craft, a person in front of a screen gradually loses the ability to feel and express for themselves. From this angle, your emptiness may not be a personal inadequacy but a result of not having been allowed to be an author for a long time. Sometimes the first step is to make something of your own, however clumsy.
emptiness.practice: Make one small thing with your own hands — draw a doodle, write three lines, hum a tune. Not for the result, but to be an author for a moment.

confusion.text: Confusion — “I don’t know what to do” — is familiar to many people today. Stiegler distinguished three kinds of knowledge: knowing how to do (craft), knowing how to live (customs, the art of being with others), and knowing how to think (theory). He believed that in an age of rapid technology all three quickly become outdated or are handed over to machines and algorithms, leaving people with the sense that they don’t understand the rules. It was this loss of knowledge that he called “proletarianization.” From this angle, your confusion isn’t stupidity but an honest reaction to a world where the old maps have stopped working. The way out, for Stiegler, is to learn anew little by little: patiently, together with others, at your own pace.
confusion.practice: Write down one thing you’re confused about, and one person or source from whom you could calmly learn something.

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout aren’t laziness but depletion. Stiegler recalled the ancient distinction between negotium — busy affairs, concern with profit — and otium — free time for reflection, friendship, art. He believed that today’s economy leaves almost no room for otium: even rest turns into consuming content, which also demands attention. Attention gets exhausted and has nowhere to recover. From this angle, burnout is both a personal misfortune and a symptom of how life as a whole is arranged. Rest that truly restores isn’t yet another series, but time when nobody wants anything from your attention.
fatigue.practice: Set aside ten minutes of real otium: no screen and no task. Look out the window, stroke an animal, listen to the quiet.

boredom.text: Boredom is unpleasant: you want to fill it with something right away. Stiegler would note that the entertainment industry is built so that boredom never gets a single second: the feed is always at hand. But, in his view, there is a price. Attention that is constantly captured from outside loses the ability to choose for itself what to rest on. Yet it is often out of a pause, out of “nothing is happening,” that your own interest is born. Stiegler drew on the psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott, who wrote about the space of play where a child invents their own world. From this angle, boredom isn’t an emptiness to be plugged immediately, but perhaps a threshold beyond which your own desire might wake up.
boredom.practice: Stay with your boredom for five minutes without picking up your phone. Notice where your attention drifts on its own.

joy.text: Joy is the feeling that life is worth living. Stiegler especially valued the figure of the amateur — someone who does something out of love rather than for gain. Music, a garden, books, a craft, friendship — everything into which long attention has been poured becomes a source of deep and inexhaustible joy. He distinguished it from the quick pleasure of consumption, which soon fades and demands the next dose. From this angle, your joy is precious, and it’s worth simply living it. And if you like, you can notice what it’s made of: perhaps there is something in it you have loved for a long time and that will go on gladdening you for a long time yet.
joy.practice: Ask yourself: what in this joy is old and beloved? Write down why you value it — as a small gift to it.

love.text: Love and tenderness are the heart of what Stiegler called desire. He distinguished desire from drive: drive wants to consume and forgets its object as soon as it is sated, while desire attaches itself to a singular, irreplaceable being and is never exhausted. For desire, the beloved doesn’t simply “exist” as a thing among things; in Stiegler’s phrase, they “consist” — they are held up by our faithfulness, attention and care. That is why love isn’t only a feeling but also a practice: it is sustained. From this angle, the tenderness you feel is one of the most precious and at the same time most fragile human capacities. It is worth caring for, like something alive.
love.practice: Do one small act of attention for a person or creature you love — something that can’t be bought: a remembered detail, a question, a touch.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a feeling in which we see how much we have been given. Stiegler described the human being as a creature that inherits not only genes but a vast world created before it: language, tools, books, skills. He called this passing-on of experience through things and signs “epiphylogenesis” — the memory of the species written outside the body. Everything you can do, and the words you think with, were given to you by others. From this angle, gratitude is a very accurate feeling: it sees the real chain of generations on which each of us rests. And it gently invites the next step — to pass something on, and to become a link in that chain yourself.
gratitude.practice: Name one person who taught you something you still use. If you can, thank them; if not, pass that skill on to someone else.

hope.text: For Stiegler, hope isn’t naivety but work. His main image is the pharmakon: something that can be both poison and remedy. The technologies that today exhaust our attention could, in principle, also nourish it — it all depends on how we handle them and how we arrange life around them. Stiegler founded the association Ars Industrialis and proposed an “economy of contribution,” in which people don’t only consume but also create, share and learn. From this angle, hope is the knowledge that poison and remedy are made of the same substance. Nothing is finally doomed if it is cared for. Your hope is already the beginning of such care.
hope.practice: Choose one thing in your life that is currently more of a “poison.” Write down how it could become even slightly more of a “remedy.”

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a longing for a past that glows in memory. Stiegler wrote a great deal about how memory works. He distinguished what we perceive right now, what we remember, and “tertiary retentions” — recordings, photographs, songs that hold the past outside us. Listening to an old song, we live it anew each time, and a little differently: memory isn’t an archive but a living process. From this angle, nostalgia isn’t an escape from the present but a way the past goes on nourishing you. Stiegler might warn only against ready-made, factory-produced nostalgia, the kind sold through remakes and advertising. Your own nostalgia, though, can be a source: it holds what truly matters to you.
nostalgia.practice: Put on a song or find a photo from that time. Ask: what in it was most precious to me — and where is that in my life now?

craving.text: A sharp craving — “I want it right now” — for a cigarette, alcohol, your phone can be very strong, and there’s nothing shameful in it. Stiegler would call what pulls at us a pharmakon — a Greek word meaning both poison and remedy. Often a substance or a device really did once make life easier: it eased anxiety, gave you a breather. But Stiegler distinguished desire, which knows how to wait and builds long bonds, from drive, which demands immediate satisfaction. Hyperconsumption, in his view, trains us precisely in drives — in the short circuit of “want it, got it.” From this angle, a craving is a wave of drive: it rises and it falls. You can wait it out, asking what kind of self-care it is trying to stand in for.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, set a timer for ten minutes and write down: what do I actually want right now — rest, comfort, company, quiet? Watch how the wave changes.

quote.text: The pharmakon is at once what enables care to be taken and that of which care must be taken.
quote.author: Bernard Stiegler
quote.source: What Makes Life Worth Living: On Pharmacology (2010)

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure. Stiegler described modern hyperconsumption as a system close to addiction: it cultivates drives in people that demand ever new doses — whether shopping, the feed or substances. Personal addiction, in this light, isn’t a strange deviation but the extreme point of where the environment keeps pushing. Every pharmakon, for Stiegler, calls for a “pharmacology” — a practice and a knowledge of how to live with it so that it doesn’t become only a poison. Such a practice is rarely built alone: for centuries it was kept by communities, rituals, traditions. From this angle, the way out of the circle isn’t a heroic effort of will but the gradual building of new supports: people, habits, places where you are cared for.
addiction.practice: Think of one support that could help you in this circle: a person, a mutual-help group, an activity. Just write it down — with no obligation to act on it right away.

hangover.text: A hangover is a hard morning, when anxiety, shame and gaps in memory are added to the body’s wreckage. This state shows very vividly what Stiegler called the double nature of the pharmakon: what seemed like relief yesterday turns into poison today. This isn’t a reason to punish yourself, just knowledge of how pharmaka work: they always have two sides. Stiegler insisted that the main thing in our relationship with any pharmakon isn’t shame but care — that is, attentive and patient treatment of yourself. Right now that care can be very simple. From this angle, the morning after isn’t a verdict, but a time to look after your body and give yourself a little gentleness before sorting out yesterday.
hangover.practice: Do one caring thing for your body — fresh air, food, rest. If yesterday is on your mind, write down one thought and set it aside until you feel better.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid high when everything seems possible. You can simply live it: it’s one of the strong human experiences. Stiegler would suggest noticing just one distinction — between what gives energy for a long time and what burns out quickly. He said that desire builds “long circuits” — bonds with people, work, plans — while drive lives by “short-circuiting.” Euphoria can become the start of something lasting: a meeting, an idea, a project. From this angle, there’s no need either to distrust it or to try to stretch it out forever. Better to ask: what would this energy like to turn into once the wave recedes? Then the flash will leave behind not ash but a trace.
euphoria.practice: Write down one idea or intention that came on this wave. Return to it tomorrow and see what you want to keep.

crash.text: The drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a bright evening — can be sharp: the world seems to fade. Stiegler would explain that much of modern life is built as an alternation of peaks: advertising, entertainment and events promise brightness, and afterward a comedown inevitably follows. This is the rhythm of drive — a short surge and a fall. Desire, by contrast, for Stiegler, works over a long distance, and its rises are gentler but steadier. From this angle, your comedown isn’t proof that everything is bad, but the natural second half of the wave. Now is not the time to draw conclusions about your life. Better to take care of yourself and wait until the ordinary, unspectacular but reliable light of everyday life returns.
crash.practice: Choose one simple, reliable thing for the next hour — a walk, a hot meal, a call to someone close. Let that be enough.

panic.text: Panic is one of the most frightening experiences: your heart pounds, you seem not to get enough air, you feel you’re losing control. It really is frightening. It can help to remember that a wave like this usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Stiegler wrote a lot about how speed and a constant stream rob us of our own rhythm, and he believed people need simple, reliable supports that give that rhythm back. From this angle, you could say that in panic you need the very first and simplest support — your body and what is right around you. There’s no need to understand or analyze anything right now. It’s enough to hold on to the present while the wave passes.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and a hand on your chest. Take a few breaths where the exhale is longer than the inhale, and name out loud five objects around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what’s the point of all this?” — comes when meanings suddenly seem hollow. Stiegler wrote about a similar state as a malaise of the era, which he called “disbelief and discredit”: when people stop believing that their life and work mean anything, a deep unease spreads. He didn’t brush this feeling aside. But his answer was practical: meaning doesn’t lie ready-made somewhere outside — it is created by attachments and by care for people, work, the world. A person, for Stiegler, builds what makes their life worthwhile themselves, and does it together with others. From this angle, your question isn’t a verdict but the start of a search carried out in small steps.
dread.practice: Write down one small thing you care for — a plant, a person, a task. Let it be your answer to “what for” today.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out is one of the most characteristic anxieties of our time, and Stiegler showed that this is no accident. He described today’s economy as an “attention economy”: its main commodity is your attention, and platforms compete for every second of it. The feed is built so that it always seems something more important is happening somewhere else than where you are. For Stiegler, this destroys the very capacity for attention — long, focused, your own. From this angle, your fear is largely produced by the environment, not by some inadequacy of yours. The life you see on the screen has been selected and edited; the life you are living has not. Its value isn’t measured by how much it resembles the feed.
fomo.practice: Put your phone away for fifteen minutes and notice what actually happened in your life during that time — not in the feed.

sleepless.text: Insomnia wears you down: at night thoughts grow louder and time drags. Stiegler wrote about how technology changes the very rhythms of our lives — attention, memory, time. From his point of view, you could notice that the rhythm of sleep is also under pressure today: screens and feeds are available around the clock, and the line between day and night is blurring. This doesn’t mean your insomnia is “because of your phone”: it can have many causes. But it is a reminder that the night is time that belongs to you, not to the stream. Night thoughts are rarely accurate: you can write them down and set them aside until morning. From this angle, you don’t have to demand that you fall asleep right away; you can gently give the night back its quiet.
sleepless.practice: If your thoughts won’t let go, write them down on paper, not on your phone, one line each, and tell yourself: “In the morning.” Then return to the feeling of the pillow and your breath.

betrayal.text: Betrayal undermines trust — not only in a person, but in the world. Stiegler wrote about “discredit” — a word in which you can hear the Latin credere, “to believe.” He held that society rests on a credit of trust: on the belief that words mean something and promises are kept. When trust collapses, the ground disappears from under your feet. On a personal level betrayal feels similar: as if you no longer know what to believe. From this angle, your pain is proportionate to the loss: something truly important has been destroyed. But trust, for Stiegler, isn’t naivety; it is something created by care, and it can be created anew — with other people, slowly, on new foundations.
betrayal.practice: Name one person you still trust, and recall what that trust rests on. Let it remind you that trust is possible.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing: the fear of losing someone mixes with pain and anger. It’s an understandable feeling — it tells you how much the person means to you. Stiegler distinguished the logic of desire from the logic of consumption. Consumption wants to possess: the thing must belong to me and be under control. Desire, in his view, is directed at the other as singular and irreplaceable — but also free. When anxiety takes over, love can quietly slide into the logic of possession, and then it hurts especially, because a person can’t be owned like a thing. From this angle, there’s no need to shame yourself for jealousy; you can notice that behind it stands a desire that needs trust, not control.
jealousy.practice: Write down what exactly you’re afraid of. Then — what you value in this person, regardless of whether they “belong” to you.

resentment.text: An old grudge is a memory that won’t let go. Stiegler thought a lot about how memory works and stressed that it is always selective. Out of a huge stream we retain only a part, and what we retain largely determines who we become. A grudge is one of those retained things: by reliving it again and again, we make it part of ourselves. From this angle, a grudge speaks not only of what was done to you, but also of how you are handling your memory now. This doesn’t mean “forgive and forget.” It means you can carefully choose what to give room to — and alongside the grudge, hold on to other things that are also true.
resentment.practice: Next to the memory of the hurt, write down one memory — from the same time or from something else in your life — that is also true but sounds different.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts almost physically. Today this pain is also surrounded by traces: messages, photos, profiles you can open at any moment. Stiegler would call them “tertiary retentions” — memory recorded outside us. They are a true pharmakon: they can comfort, and they can reopen the wound again and again. This doesn’t mean you need to delete them right away: the decision is yours and may come later. But it helps to notice at which moments they heal and at which they hurt. From Stiegler’s point of view, the love that was is real: it left a trace in who you have become. Grieving it is also a form of care for what was precious.
heartbreak.practice: Before you open the messages or photos, ask yourself: will this be a remedy or a poison for me right now? Just notice the answer.

impostor.text: Impostor syndrome is exhausting: it seems you’re only pretending to know, and soon it will come out. Stiegler would help you see more here than a personal fear. He wrote about the “proletarianization of knowledge”: in today’s world knowledge is increasingly stored in systems, algorithms and instructions, and an individual often feels they don’t really understand anything themselves. This feeling is very widespread, and it says a lot about the environment, not about your worth. Stiegler valued the figure of the amateur — someone who learns out of love and isn’t obliged to know everything in advance. From this angle, you’re not an impostor but a learner. Knowledge isn’t issued once and for all — it is constantly being won, and doubt is part of that path.
impostor.practice: Write down one thing you truly know how to do and learned yourself. Remember how it, too, was once new to you.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred is one of the heaviest forms of pain. The voice that condemns you is loud, but that doesn’t mean it’s right. Stiegler believed that every person needs love of self — following psychoanalysis, he called it “primary narcissism.” This isn’t vanity, but a basic sense that you have a right to be and that your existence has value. Without it, it’s impossible either to love others or to care for the world. Stiegler saw that today’s environment — comparisons, ratings, advertisements for perfect lives — constantly erodes this foundation. From this angle, your pain isn’t proof that you’re worthless but a sign that this foundation has been wounded. And what is wounded can be healed with care.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic. Next to it, write how someone who loves you would answer it.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is agonizing: you see what’s happening and can’t change it. Stiegler knew powerlessness from the inside: he spent several years in a prison cell where almost nothing depended on him. Later he said that it was there he began reading philosophy and turned his cell into a place of study: he couldn’t change his circumstances, but he could change his relationship to time and attention. He didn’t romanticize prison, but the experience convinced him that even in a very narrow space a tiny freedom remains — the freedom of attention. From this angle, your helplessness is real, but it doesn’t cancel everything. Somewhere nearby there is a small area in which you can still act.
helplessness.practice: Divide a page into two parts: “what isn’t in my power” and “one tiny thing that is.” Do that thing today.

procrastination.text: Procrastination isn’t laziness. Stiegler would point out that our attention today is under constant attack: apps and feeds are designed to capture it, and they do so professionally. Fighting them with “willpower” alone is like arguing with an entire industry. Besides, tasks that require long attention — “long circuits,” as Stiegler would say — don’t give satisfaction right away, and the drive toward quick reward pulls you away. From this angle, procrastination isn’t your personal defect but a struggle for your own attention that everyone knows. What helps isn’t shame but gently adjusting your surroundings: the fewer lures nearby, the easier it is for your attention to return to the task.
procrastination.practice: Put your phone in another room for fifteen minutes and take the very smallest first step of the task. Just that.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — a move, emigration — is the loss not only of a place but of a whole environment in which you knew how to live. Drawing on Simondon, Stiegler distinguished an “associated” milieu, in which a person takes part, which they understand and can change, from a “dissociated” one, where they are only a consumer and an outsider. In a new place almost everything feels dissociated at first: you don’t know the rules and don’t take part in the life around you. From this angle, your sense of being lost is natural: it is the loss of the “knowing how to live” that was second nature in your old place. But an associated milieu can be built anew — through participation, small habits, people with whom you do things together.
uprooted.practice: Find one place or community nearby where you could not just be present, but gradually take part.

overload.text: Overload — the endless feed, notifications, news — leaves your head overfull and yet strangely empty. Stiegler, following Plato and Derrida, would remind you that writing itself was already a pharmakon. In the Phaedrus, Socrates retells a myth in which an Egyptian king warns that writing will weaken memory — and yet without writing there would be no philosophy. Today the digital stream has become the pharmakon. It can expand the mind or exhaust it: when there is more information than attention can process, we learn not more but less. From this angle, overload isn’t a sign of your weakness but a natural reaction to a stream designed to capture attention. It needs boundaries — not a rejection of technology, but your own rhythm for dealing with it.
overload.practice: Choose one app and turn off its notifications for today. In the evening, notice what you actually missed.

quote.text: You have not discovered a potion for remembering, but for reminding.
quote.author: Plato

unreality.text: The sense of unreality — as if the world were behind glass, or you yourself were in a dream — can be very unsettling. Stiegler would offer one angle on this feeling, without claiming to explain it all. He wrote that more and more of our experience passes through screens and recordings: we see the world “as a broadcast,” and increasingly we turn our experiences straight into snapshots and posts. When perception is so heavily mediated, direct contact with things can weaken, and the world seems flat. From this angle, unreality may partly be a sign that your attention lacks the immediate. You can gently bring it back — through the body, through touch, through simple things done with your hands that no one needs to see.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — wood, fabric, cool water — and for a minute describe the sensation to yourself, without photographing anything.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — stars, mountains, music — is a rare and precious experience. Stiegler said that the most important things for human beings — justice, beauty, love — don’t “exist” the way things exist: they can’t be bought or put in a pocket. Such things, in his phrase, “consist” — they are held up by our attention, faithfulness and care, and are therefore inexhaustible. Awe is a moment when we touch this inexhaustible. Stiegler contrasted such experiences with consumption, which quickly exhausts its object. From this angle, your wonder is one of the most living forms of desire. It doesn’t need to be explained or hastily captured. You can simply breathe it.
awe.practice: For one minute, look at what fills you with awe, without taking a photo. Then recall it with your eyes closed.

relief.text: Relief is the breath out after long tension, and you can simply live it. Stiegler would note that our attention is usually stretched like a string: tasks, notifications and worries constantly pull it in different directions. In relief the string finally slackens, and you can see how much strength was going into holding on. From this angle, relief is a precious moment when your attention comes back to you. There’s no need to fill the freed-up space right away with a new feed or a new task. Stiegler valued otium — free time that belongs to no one and is filled with nothing. Relief is a good reason to give yourself a little of that time.
relief.practice: Without picking up your phone, sit for three minutes and notice where in your body you feel the relief. Let this time belong to no one.

calm.text: Calm is a rare state, especially in a world where so much is built to excite and distract us. Stiegler considered attention one of the most important human values and stressed that it is formed slowly, in quiet and concentration — the way a child learns to listen to a story to the end. Calm is attention that nothing is disturbing and that isn’t hurrying anywhere. From this angle, your calm isn’t emptiness or idleness but the restoring of a capacity Stiegler saw as the basis of thought, care and love. You can simply enjoy it, without thinking about what to fill it with. Calm produces nothing, and that is its value.
calm.practice: Choose a sound you can hear right now, and for a minute simply listen to it, without judging or naming it.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the feeling that something wants to come into the world through you. For Stiegler this is one of the most important human capacities: to be not only a consumer of others’ images and meanings but their author. He said that “symbolic misery” arises when people stop taking part in creating culture. Inspiration is the opposite of that misery: a moment when your sensibility becomes your own again. Stiegler valued amateurs — those who create out of love rather than for the market. From this angle, inspiration doesn’t have to be “professional” or useful. It is valuable as an act of taking part in the world. Best to catch it and start making while it’s still breathing.
inspiration.practice: Right now, write down or sketch whatever came — messily and without editing. It’s a draft, not an exam.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — the quiet joy when something didn’t work out for someone else — is one of the most hidden feelings, and almost everyone knows it. Stiegler didn’t write about it directly, but his analysis of the “attention economy” sheds a lot of light here. Digital platforms, in his view, constantly put us on display in front of one another and turn life into a feed of comparisons, where another’s success feels like your own loss. Stiegler distinguished desire, which is directed at something of your own and knows how to wait, from drive — a short “here and now” impulse. From this angle, you could say schadenfreude is a quick discharge of the drive to compare: for a moment it seems you’ve won. The feeling itself says nothing about what kind of person you are. But it can hint at where your own desire has been overshadowed by other people’s results.
schadenfreude.practice: Recall whose failure recently pleased you, and write down: what do I want in this area — not in comparison, but for myself?

contempt.text: Contempt is hard to admit: it seems cold and arrogant. But it almost always has a reason — tiredness, disappointment, hurt at someone else’s carelessness. In States of Shock: Stupidity and Knowledge in the 21st Century (2012), Stiegler, following Deleuze, reflects on “stupidity” (in French, bêtise) and insists that it isn’t only a property of “others” but a possibility shared by everyone, philosophers included. Knowledge, in his view, is born precisely from the encounter with one’s own stupidity, not from superiority over someone else’s. From this angle, you could say contempt is an attempt to move stupidity entirely outside, into another person, so as not to notice it in yourself. This isn’t a verdict on you: it’s simply easier that way. But if you see that the line runs through each of us, contempt can give way to something more alive — interest, argument, care for what hurt you.
contempt.practice: Think of a person you currently feel contempt for, and write down one situation where you were even a little like them. Not for self-flagellation — just to soften the line.

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily “no”: to a person, a situation, sometimes to yourself. It’s unpleasant, but it carries important information. Stiegler wrote about “symbolic misery” — the impoverishment of our ability to feel and create meanings for ourselves when our tastes and desires are supplied by the marketing industry. He called this “aesthetic conditioning”: sensibility tuned from the outside, like the temperature in a room. From this angle, you could say disgust is a sign that your sensibility is alive and resisting: something in you refuses to accept just anything. Even disgust with yourself often speaks not of your being “spoiled,” but of a mismatch with an image imposed from outside. There’s no need to inflate disgust or be ashamed of it. You can question it: what exactly is it protecting you from, and what do you really value?
disgust.practice: Name what you feel disgust toward right now, and finish the sentence: “What matters to me is that instead there would be…”. Disgust often points to what is dear to you.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge comes when you’ve been wounded and the wound demands an answer. This feeling is understandable: it says you were treated unjustly. Stiegler distinguished “short circuits” from “long circuits.” A short circuit is a drive that demands immediate discharge: you were hit — hit back. A long circuit is a path on which the impulse passes through time, words, other people and memory, and turns into something shared: a demand for justice, a story, a change in the rules. For Stiegler it is precisely such long circuits that make us human, and the industry of instant reactions keeps shortening them. From this angle, the thirst for revenge is the raw energy of hurt. There’s no need to be ashamed of it, and no need to act on it by causing harm. It can be channeled into a long circuit: naming the injustice and seeking to have it acknowledged.
revenge.practice: Write down in one or two sentences what exactly was unjust — without any plans for retaliation. Then ask yourself: whom could I tell about this so that it is heard?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at people close to you is especially painful: you love them — and suddenly you snap, and then you feel ashamed. It’s a very common feeling, and it doesn’t cancel love. In Taking Care of Youth and the Generations, Stiegler wrote that attention isn’t only a personal capacity but something formed between people, above all in the family and between generations. And today’s industry, in his view, hijacks attention: screens, notifications, endless urgency. When there’s no attention left, those close to us start to be felt as just one more demand among many. From this angle, you could say anger is a signal of depleted attention, not proof that you’re a bad partner or parent. It’s no reason to take it out on anyone. But it is a reason to look after what your attention feeds on, and how.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, ask yourself: how much attention do I have left right now, from 0 to 10? If it’s less than three, take five minutes of screen-free quiet before continuing the conversation.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and not being able to stand them is a very human combination, even though it’s frightening to admit. Stiegler had an exact word for such doubleness — pharmakon. In Greek it means both poison and remedy. Stiegler applied it above all to technology, but the logic itself is broader: one and the same thing can both nourish and poison, depending on the measure and on how it is handled. From this angle, you could say a person close to you can be a pharmakon too: they give you support — and they also wear you out. Your ambivalence isn’t a mistake of feeling or a sign that the love is “not real.” It is an honest perception of complexity. Stiegler understood care as the art of handling a pharmakon: not rejecting it entirely and not taking it without measure, but looking for a form in which there is more remedy than poison.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page into two columns: “what this person gives me” and “what in me gets tired of them.” Don’t choose between them — just look at both.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after someone leaves, after a breakup, or after a loved one’s long illness can be mixed with shame: how can you feel lightness if you love? But one doesn’t cancel the other. Stiegler wrote a great deal about care — in French, soin — as the central human practice: caring for children, for memory, for the world, for oneself. Care, in his view, is also a pharmakon, both remedy and poison: it nourishes the bond and can exhaust the one who cares, especially when they lack support. Long strain — waiting, sleepless nights, constant readiness — settles into the body. When it ends, the body lets go. From this angle, relief isn’t a betrayal of love but the natural response of someone who has carried a weight for a long time. Love and relief can live side by side, and you can allow yourself both.
guilty_relief.practice: Say to yourself out loud, or write: “The love was there and still is — and I feel lighter. Both are true.”

indifference.text: Sometimes, where you “ought” to be moved — someone else’s grief, an important event, even your own celebration — there is silence inside. It’s frightening, but there is an explanation. In Disbelief and Discredit, Stiegler wrote about the désaffectés — people from whom industrial culture gradually takes away the capacity to be affected. The French word is double-edged: it means both “deprived of affect” and “disused,” like an abandoned building. The stream of images, news and stimuli is so dense that sensibility protects itself by going numb. This is part of what Stiegler called “symbolic misery.” From this angle, your indifference isn’t coldness of character but perhaps the fatigue of a sensibility overloaded beyond measure. It doesn’t mean you truly don’t care. Feeling often comes back not on command, but when it is given time and quiet.
indifference.practice: Choose one impression from today — a sound, a face, a taste — and stay with it for a minute without your phone. Notice whether anything inside responds, even faintly.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your familiar role — can be sudden and very strong. This isn’t about leaving life, but about the wish to live differently. Stiegler described “proletarianization” — not only poverty, but the loss of your own knowledge, when work comes down to carrying out someone else’s procedures and leisure to consuming ready-made things. He recalled the ancient distinction between negotium — business, being occupied — and otium, free time for thought, creativity and care of oneself, which, in his view, modern industry also turns into a commodity. From this angle, the wish to escape is a longing for otium, for time that would be yours again. You don’t have to change your circumstances right away. You can start with a question: where do I still have even a little time of my own — and what is taking it away?
escape.practice: Write down two answers: “What exactly do I want to escape from?” and “What am I missing there — time, meaning, the chance to do something of my own?” You don’t need to decide anything.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “the wrong person” often comes uninvited and is unsettling. This feeling speaks of a living desire, not of your being corrupt. Following Freud, Stiegler distinguished drive from desire. Drive seeks immediate satisfaction. Desire is attached to something singular, unrepeatable, and is capable of sublimation — Freud’s word for turning the energy of drive into creativity, friendship, thought, work. Stiegler considered this capacity precious and saw how a culture of instant consumption erodes it. From this angle, you could say such an attraction points to something you need to touch: aliveness, recognition, another version of yourself. There’s no need to decide anything right now — in either direction. You can simply ask yourself what this desire is about — it may tell you more than it seems.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down in one to three words what this attraction promises you. Then ask yourself where else in your life that promise might be heard.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is familiar to very many: your throat tightens, you want to hide. This isn’t weakness but sensitivity to how you are seen. Stiegler described the human being through “individuation” — an ongoing becoming-oneself that happens not alone but together with others; he called it “psychic and collective individuation.” That’s why the gaze of others means so much to us. But Stiegler warned that digital platforms turn this togetherness into constant counting: likes, ratings, views. Evaluation becomes the background of your whole life, and even a live conversation starts to feel like a test. From this angle, your anxiety isn’t only a personal trait but also a reaction to an environment where we are continuously measured. Real contact isn’t an exam but a shared becoming, in which you have a voice too.
social_anxiety.practice: Think of one person around whom you are listened to rather than judged. What is different about that contact? Write down one detail.

uncertainty.text: When it’s unclear what will happen, it’s hard to make plans, and the body lives in tension. That’s a natural reaction. Stiegler distinguished two French words: devenir — “becoming,” what simply happens on its own — and avenir — “the future,” what people desire, imagine and create together. He believed that an era of rapid technological change floods us with becoming, leaving almost no room for the future: everything changes, yet it seems we choose nothing. From this angle, uncertainty isn’t only an anxious fog but also a space in which the future hasn’t yet been taken. You don’t have to know what will happen. You can ask yourself what small step today would make the future a little more yours, rather than something that merely happened.
uncertainty.practice: Write down one thing you don’t know right now, and next to it one small step you can take without knowing the answer.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, for results, for news — is exhausting: time drags, and there’s almost nothing you can do. Stiegler didn’t romanticize such torment at all, but he valued the very human capacity to wait. For him it is precisely what distinguishes desire from drive: drive demands “right now,” while desire knows how to defer and hold out through the interval. Stiegler studied with Jacques Derrida, for whom deferral is woven into the very fabric of meaning. And today’s industry, according to Stiegler, trains us in instantaneity: notifications, one-hour delivery, the endlessly refreshing feed. That’s why waiting is especially hard to bear today — we’ve been trained out of it. From this angle, your restlessness is understandable, and the ability to dwell in the interval can be recovered little by little. Waiting isn’t empty time: in it you can care for what is within your reach now.
waiting.practice: Choose one small task that can be finished today while you wait — and do it slowly, without checking your phone.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do can come back again and again. It shows that the past matters to you. Stiegler thought a great deal about memory and singled out a special kind — “tertiary retentions”: memory carried outside us, into recordings, photos, letters, diaries. His important idea: the past doesn’t lie still. Each time we return to it, we select and interpret it anew — and by that selection we are already choosing what our future will be. A person, for Stiegler, is an unfinished “individuation,” a process rather than a final result. From this angle, your regret isn’t a verdict but material: you can build your next step from it. The past can’t be changed, but you can change how it works in you — what lessons you choose from it and what you decide to carry forward.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and below it what this experience showed about your values. This isn’t an excuse, but a different reading of the same story.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is one of the most precise feelings: you don’t need “someone,” you need exactly him or her. Stiegler gave this enormous importance. Desire, in his view, is always directed at the singular — at what cannot be replaced. Consumer culture teaches the opposite, interchangeability: everything can be upgraded, a substitute found, scrolled past. From this angle, your longing is a quiet resistance to that logic. It testifies that the capacity for what Stiegler called desire in the proper sense — attachment to the unrepeatable — is alive in you. Longing hurts, and there’s no need to prettify that. But it isn’t a sign of weakness: it is a form of faithfulness to what was dear to you. In time it can become a memory that not only wounds but also warms.
longing.practice: Write down three things that were unrepeatable about this particular person. Let yourself feel gratitude for them, even if the sadness remains.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — for the wars, disasters and injustice the news reports every day — is heavy, and there is nothing excessive about it. In his late works Stiegler wrote about an era of “disruption” — rapid ruptures that neither laws, nor feelings, nor thought can keep up with. He spoke of the “Entropocene” — a time when humanity is exhausting its resources, including its inner ones. A nonstop stream of alarming news, in his view, overloads attention and leaves a person powerless before the scale of what is happening. But Stiegler also looked for an answer — “negentropy”: local actions that create order, meaning and care in the face of decay. From this angle, you don’t have to carry the whole world alone. Your pain is a sign that you care, and it can be turned into small acts of care close to you.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small act of care for today — near you and within your strength. And give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply: as if you’d been told there is no place for you. In To Love, to Love Oneself, to Love Us (2003), Stiegler wrote that life requires “primary narcissism” — a healthy, basic love of self, without which it is impossible to love others. This love isn’t born in isolation: it grows out of how we are accepted, listened to, reflected back. That’s why a refusal hurts so much — it strikes exactly at this support. But Stiegler has another idea too: individuation, our becoming ourselves, runs through many bonds, not through one. From this angle, rejection by one person or one group is the breaking of one thread, not a verdict on the whole fabric. Your pain is real. And at the same time it doesn’t define your worth.
rejection.practice: List the people, activities and places you are connected with — at least five. Notice: one thread has broken, but the fabric is wider.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned has very deep roots — in the very beginning of life, when we depend entirely on others. Stiegler considered this dependence not a weakness but the essence of being human. A person is born helpless and becomes themselves only thanks to care: adults pass on language, memory and skills. Stiegler drew on the psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott, who wrote about how a child learns to bear the mother’s absence with the help of a “transitional object” — a favorite toy or blanket. Such things, for Stiegler, are the first supports we find outside ourselves. From this angle, the fear of being left without support is an echo of that original dependence, not a sign that you are “too much.” In adult life, too, supports can be multiplied: people, activities, places and habits that hold you when any one person drifts away.
abandonment.practice: Recall your adult “transitional object” — a thing, place or ritual that calms you. Turn to it today, deliberately and gently.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts doubly: the feeling is there, but there is no answer. This isn’t “foolishness” or a sign that something is wrong with you. Stiegler distinguished what “exists” from what “consists” (in French, consister). The objects of our deep desire — love, justice, beauty — never fully exist as things that can be obtained, but they “consist”: they act in us, guide us and hold us. From this angle, you could say your love is real even if it has met no answer: it has already changed you, taught you attention and tenderness. Stiegler considered the capacity for such desire precious, especially in a world where everything comes down to quick acquisition. There’s no need to rush the pain. In time, what you discovered in yourself may find a new addressee.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has taught you — what tenderness, what kind of attention. That remains yours, regardless of the answer.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if you’d been stripped of your dignity in front of others. Stiegler wrote that people need not only food and safety but also a share in the common world of symbols — words, images, meanings, where their voice counts for something. Being deprived of that share he called “symbolic misery.” Humiliation works in a similar way: it tries to push you out of the circle of those whose voice counts. Stiegler insisted that the symbolic world doesn’t belong only to the powerful: it is made by everyone who speaks, writes, remembers, tells stories. From this angle, humiliation speaks of the actions of those who humiliated you, not of your worth. What helps you reclaim your dignity is precisely speech: naming what happened in your own words and being heard by at least one person.
humiliation.practice: Tell one person you trust about what happened — or write it down for yourself, calling things by their names.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is familiar to very many people, and it isn’t your fault. Stiegler wrote about “temporal objects” — films, shows, videos that unfold in time and capture our consciousness while we watch them. The industry, in his view, “synchronizes” millions of consciousnesses: everyone watches the same thing at the same time and gradually begins to desire the same things. That is how a single image of the “right” body takes shape — selected, retouched, repeated thousands of times. We compare our living body with it, though no one has retouched ours. From this angle, your dissatisfaction is largely an echo of other people’s pictures, not the truth about you. The antidote is to reclaim your own perception: to notice what your body can do, feel and remember, not only how it looks.
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body did for you today — for example, carried you, kept you warm, let you taste something. No judgments about appearance.

illness.text: When the body lets you down, the familiar sense that it simply “works” collapses. It’s frightening and exhausting, and your feelings here are legitimate. Stiegler held that human beings were never self-sufficient bodies: from the very beginning we have lived through “prostheses” in the broad sense — tools, glasses, records, other people’s care. For him this isn’t humiliating but human nature itself. Stiegler also drew on the philosopher of medicine Georges Canguilhem: health isn’t simply the absence of illness, but the capacity to create new norms of life, adapting to changed conditions. From this angle, illness doesn’t cancel you: it calls for inventing a new routine, new supports, a new measure of strength. This doesn’t have to be done heroically. Small steps and a willingness to accept help are enough.
illness.practice: Write down one support that helps you right now — a person, a thing or a habit. Allow yourself to lean on it a little more today.

pride.text: Pride in something you’ve done is a good feeling, and there’s no need to hide it out of modesty. Stiegler held the figure of the amateur in high regard — in French, amateur, from the word for “to love”: someone who does something out of love for it, not only for the result or the pay. He believed that the industrial era turns people into operators and consumers, taking away their own knowledge. So the moment when you yourself have created, mastered or finished something matters doubly for Stiegler: it is a reclaiming of knowledge and a step in your individuation — your becoming yourself. From this angle, pride is a sign that you took part in your own life rather than just consuming it. You can give it a place: without exaggerating or brushing it off, notice what you learned along the way.
pride.practice: Write down what exactly you did and what you learned along the way. Read it again — and let yourself be glad, without brushing it off.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet, almost tender feeling, when you’re sad but not weighed down. There’s no need to chase it away or cure it. Stiegler loved an example borrowed from the philosopher Edmund Husserl: a melody. We hear a melody rather than separate sounds because we are still holding on to the notes that have sounded and already anticipating the next ones. Our consciousness works the same way: the present is always woven from echoes of the past and expectations of the future. Melancholy is a moment when these threads become audible: the past sounds within the present, like a fading melody. From this angle, your bright sadness is a sign of a deep, “long” time within you, so rarely available in the rush of modern life. Stiegler would call such a state the opposite of a “short circuit.” You can simply stay in it for a while.
melancholy.practice: Put on a melody that resonates with this mood and listen to it from beginning to end, without doing anything else at the same time.
